title: The woman at the market (Gaudete et Exsultate 16)
hookLine: holiness grows by small gestures, like refusing to gossip
tomorrow: what does a pope tell the young first, before any advice?

lines: A SCREENSHOT IN THE GROUP CHAT.
cards: Somebody in the group chat posts a screenshot about a person who isn't in the chat. The replies start stacking up. Your thumb is over the keyboard.
Pope Francis tells a scene like that, minus the phone, in Gaudete et Exsultate, Rejoice and Be Glad, his letter on the call to holiness. A woman goes shopping.
At the market she runs into a neighbor, they start to talk, and the gossip starts. And she says in her heart: no, I won't speak badly of anyone.

teach.b: Francis calls that silent no a step forward in holiness. Then he follows her home. One of her children wants to talk about his hopes and dreams.
She's tired. She sits down and listens anyway. Another step.
Later, anxious, she remembers the love of the Virgin Mary, takes her rosary and prays with faith. Another step.
Out on the street, she meets a poor man and stops to say a kind word. One more. Nothing in her day would make the news, and that's the point.
Holiness, Francis says, grows through small gestures.
Earlier in the same letter he names the saints next door: parents raising children with love, people working hard for their families, the sick, elderly religious who never lose their smile.
And look how her day begins. Her first step isn't a deed. It's a sentence she decides not to say.

how: Catholics who read Gaudete et Exsultate take holiness as something lived in ordinary days: a held tongue, a patient ear, a prayer, a kind word.

games.q: what does “the woman at the market” mean?
o: Francis's picture of holiness in an ordinary day
a saint who ran a market stall for the poor
a Gospel story about Jesus clearing the Temple

games.q: her day of small steps — tap the pairs.
p: she won't speak badly of anyone
she listens to her child, though tired
a kind word to a poor man

s: in Gaudete et Exsultate, holiness is mostly for heroes and great deeds
Francis says it grows through small gestures, and names the saints next door.
the woman's first step toward holiness is something she doesn't say
a silent no to gossip, at the market.
Francis says the saints next door are mainly priests and nuns
he names parents, workers, the sick, and elderly religious who keep smiling.

games.q: a friend vents to you about a coworker, and it's sliding into mocking him. you don't want to lecture her. what's the market woman's move?
o: laugh along this once so she doesn't feel judged.
quietly don't add anything bad, and steer back to how she's doing.
tell her gossip is a sin and end the conversation.
games.why: her step was a silent no: she didn't preach; she just refused to speak badly of anyone. small, and Francis calls it holiness.

practice: Say her sentence out loud, once, quietly: no, I won't speak badly of anyone. Then let one person come to mind who often gets talked about when they're not in the room, and simply hold them there, kindly, for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: The woman at the market. Francis's picture of ordinary holiness: a day built out of small, hidden gestures.

orig.note: Latin: rejoice and be glad, words of Jesus in Matthew 5:12 and the title of Francis's letter.

carryVoice: Keep this one: small gestures, starting with a sentence you decide to leave unsaid. That's the week.
